Welcome

A visual, cross-linked rewrite of your Obsidian vault — the journey from Pre-Security foundations through Cyber Security 101, SOC Level 1, and the hands-on Advent of Cyber 2025 labs, distilled into diagrams, comparison tables, and highlighted key concepts.

How to use this handbook

  • Collapsible contents — the sidebar is a three-level tree. Collapse or expand by Part (learning path), by Topic (chapter), or drill into sub-topics. Use Expand all / Collapse all at the top to flip the whole tree at once. On a phone, tap ☰.
  • Search — type in the search box to filter the contents to matching topics; matches are highlighted and their chapters auto-expand.
  • Light / dark — use the ◐ Theme button (top-right) to switch; your choice is remembered.
  • Colour-coded by path — each Part has its own colour so you always know where you are:

Pre-Security foundations   CS 101 core skills   SOC L1 blue team   Advent of Cyber hands-on labs   Reference quick lookups

  • Cross-links — within the text, links like this jump to related topics.
  • Nothing is lost — anything trimmed from your original notes is preserved verbatim in The Noise at the end.

A faster or safer way.

1 · Security Mindset, Careers & the CIA Triad

Offensive vs Defensive Security

Cyber security splits into two complementary mindsets. The offensive side thinks like an attacker to find weaknesses; the defensive side monitors, detects and responds to protect systems.

The core idea

"To outsmart a hacker, you need to think like one." Offensive security breaks into systems to find flaws before criminals do. Defensive security (blue teaming) builds and watches the walls.

Offensive Security (Red) Defensive Security (Blue)
Goal Think like an attacker to find flaws first Protect networks, detect intrusions, respond
Mindset "To outsmart a hacker, think like one." "Defence in depth" — layered controls
Typical work Breaking in, exploiting bugs, finding loopholes Monitoring, incident response, threat intel
Example tool Gobuster brute-forcing hidden pages SIEM correlating logs; IDS; firewalls

Your first hack (the FakeBank lab)

gobuster brute-forces hidden web directories from a wordlist, revealing an unprotected /bank-transfer admin page — a real-world access control failure. Status: 200 means the page exists; if an admin left it public, an attacker finds it — and an ethical hacker reports it before a criminal abuses it.

gobuster -u http://fakebank.thm -w wordlist.txt dir
# -u  target URL      -w  wordlist      dir  directory brute-force mode
# Status: 200 = page exists   301 = redirect

Defence in Depth

Organisations never rely on one control. They layer them like an onion or a castle's walls, so that if one fails, others still hold.

Defensive layer Role
Employee training Humans are the most-attacked surface; teach phishing awareness
IDS (Intrusion Detection System) "Surveillance cameras" that alert on suspicious activity
Firewalls "Security guards" deciding what traffic may enter/leave
Security policies Rules (strong passwords, blocked sites) that shrink the attack surface

The five defensive responsibilities: Monitoring & Detecting · Incident Response · Threat Intelligence · Vulnerability Management · Investigation & Analysis.

The Cyber Careers Map

Role One-line summary Key metric / skill
Security Analyst Maintains an organisation's data security; builds measures across teams Reporting, risk analysis
Security Engineer Designs & maintains controls, networks, systems Threat & vuln data
Incident Responder Mitigates attacks while they unfold MTTD / MTTA / MTTR
Digital Forensics Examiner Investigates incidents & crimes from digital evidence Legal chain of custody
Malware Analyst Reverse-engineers malicious programs Assembly, C, static+dynamic analysis
Penetration Tester Tests products for exploitable flaws (with permission) Systemised hacking, reporting
Red Teamer Emulates a real adversary to test detection & response Stealth, persistence, evasion

Incident-response timing metrics

  • MTTD — Mean Time to Detect: average time to identify a threat.
  • MTTA — Mean Time to Acknowledge: time from alert to an analyst taking action.
  • MTTR — Mean Time to Respond: time from alert to the breach being stopped (malware removal, password reset, restore).

The CIA Triad

Everything in cyber security protects three properties of data. This is the model you will return to constantly.

Pillar Protects against Achieved? — example
Confidentiality Eavesdropping, data theft Gmail creds on a sticky note → No · internal docs limited to staff who need them → Yes
Integrity Unauthorised modification Grades changed after lock → No · change via approved process → Yes
Availability Downtime, DoS Site offline in business hours → No · systems reachable during work hours → Yes

Why it matters

When you triage an alert or assess a risk, ask which pillar is threatened. Ransomware attacks Availability (and often Confidentiality); a defaced website attacks Integrity; a leaked database attacks Confidentiality.

2 · Networking Fundamentals

A network is simply things connected. In computing, anywhere from 2 to billions of devices communicate using shared rules (protocols).

Identifying Devices: IP & MAC

Every device has two identifiers — like a changeable name and a permanent fingerprint.

Identifier Analogy Changeable? Format
IP address Your name (can change) Yes — reassigned over time 192.168.1.77 (4 octets, IPv4)
MAC address Your fingerprint / serial Burnt in at factory (but spoofable) a4:c3:f0:85:ac:2d (12 hex chars)

Private vs Public IP

A private IP identifies a device within a local network (e.g. 192.168.1.74). A public IP identifies your whole network on the Internet and is issued by your ISP. Many devices share one public IP.

IPv4 vs IPv6

IPv4 has 2³² ≈ 4.29 billion addresses — nearly exhausted. IPv6 uses 2¹²⁸ (≈ 340 trillion-plus) addresses and is more efficient. A MAC's first 6 hex chars identify the manufacturer; the last 6 are unique. MAC addresses can be spoofed, breaking security that trusts them (e.g. café Wi-Fi allow-lists).

The OSI Model

The Open Systems Interconnection model is the 7-layer framework describing how all networked devices send, receive and interpret data. Each layer adds its own information — a process called encapsulation.

Remember the layers

All People Seem To Need Data Processing (7→1). Layer 6 is the translator (and where encryption like HTTPS lives). Firewalls operate at layers 3 & 4.

Layer Deals with Devices / examples
7 Application How the user interacts with data Browsers, email clients, DNS
6 Presentation Standardising & encrypting data HTTPS/TLS, data formats
5 Session Opening/closing/maintaining sessions Checkpoints to resume lost data
4 Transport TCP vs UDP, ports, error-checking Port numbers
3 Network Routing via IP addresses Routers (Layer-3 devices)
2 Data Link Physical MAC addressing NIC, Layer-2 switches, frames
1 Physical Raw bits on the wire Ethernet cables

Packets & Frames

Packet vs Frame

A packet is Layer-3 data: an IP header + payload. A frame is Layer-2: it encapsulates the packet and adds MAC addresses. Think of mailing a letter — the envelope is the frame, the letter inside is the packet.

Data is split into small pieces so a network doesn't bottleneck. Key IP headers: Time To Live (expiry), Checksum (integrity), Source Address, Destination Address.

TCP vs UDP

Layer 4 chooses between two transport protocols.

TCP UDP
Connection Establishes one first (handshake) None — stateless
Reliability Guarantees accuracy & order No guarantee; data may be lost
Speed Slower (more processing) Much faster
Use cases File sharing, web, email Video/voice streaming, ARP, DHCP

The TCP Three-Way Handshake

TCP must establish a connection before sending data, synchronising sequence numbers so pieces reassemble in order.

Key TCP flags

SYN initiate & synchronise · SYN/ACK server acknowledges · ACK acknowledges received data · DATA carries the payload · FIN cleanly closes · RST abruptly ends (last resort / error).

Important TCP headers include Source/Destination Port, Source/Destination IP, Sequence Number, Acknowledgement Number, Checksum (integrity), Data, and Flag.

Ports

Ports are numbered endpoints (0–65535) that let a device run many services at once. Ports 0–1024 are "common" and standardised.

Port Protocol Purpose
21 FTP File transfer (client-server)
22 SSH Secure remote text login/management
80 HTTP The World Wide Web (unencrypted)
443 HTTPS HTTP with encryption
445 SMB File & printer sharing
3389 RDP Remote graphical desktop

Non-standard ports

Standards are conventions, not rules — a web server can run on 8080. To reach it you must specify the port with a colon: http://site.com:8080.

Ping / ICMP

ping uses ICMP echo request/reply packets to test whether a host is reachable and measure round-trip time.

ping 192.168.1.254    # or ping tryhackme.com

3 · LANs, Devices & Network Extension

LAN Topologies

The topology is the design or shape of a network. Each has trade-offs.

Topology Pros Cons
Star Scalable, reliable, easy to add devices Costly (cabling + hardware); central device is a single point of failure
Bus Cheap, simple Backbone bottlenecks; one cable break kills it; hard to troubleshoot
Ring Little cabling, less bottlenecking, easy fault isolation Inefficient (data hops many devices); one break halts the ring

Switches & Routers

Switch vs Router

A switch aggregates many devices (ports of 4–64) on one network and forwards frames to the correct device by MAC address (Layer 2) — far more efficient than a hub, which repeats to everyone. A router connects different networks and passes data between them by routing packets (Layer 3), choosing paths by shortest/most-reliable/fastest medium.

A Layer-3 switch can do some routing. VLANs (Virtual LANs) virtually split devices on one switch so, e.g., Sales and Accounting share Internet but cannot talk to each other — adding security segmentation.

ARP — Address Resolution Protocol

ARP maps an IP address → MAC address so devices can actually deliver frames. Each device keeps an ARP cache.

DHCP

Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol automatically assigns IP addresses. The exchange is DORA:

Subnetting

Subnetting splits one network into smaller logical networks. A subnet mask (32 bits, each octet 0–255) decides how many hosts fit.

Type Purpose Example
Network Address Identifies the network's start 192.168.1.0
Host Address Identifies a device on the subnet 192.168.1.100
Default Gateway Device that forwards traffic to other networks 192.168.1.254 (first/last host)

Why subnet?

Efficiency, security, and control. A café separates its public Wi-Fi subnet from the staff/till subnet while both still reach the Internet.

Extending the Network

Firewalls

A firewall is border security for a network — it permits or denies traffic by source, destination, port, and protocol, performing packet inspection. It operates at OSI layers 3 & 4.

Firewall type Inspects Trade-off
Stateful The entire connection (dynamic) Resource-heavy; blocks a whole device if a connection is bad
Stateless Individual packets against static rules Cheap & fast but "dumber"; great against DDoS from many hosts

VPNs

A Virtual Private Network creates an encrypted tunnel so devices on separate networks communicate securely as one private network.

VPN benefits

Connects geographically-separate networks · Privacy (encryption defeats sniffing, useful on public Wi-Fi) · Anonymity (only as good as the provider's logging policy).

VPN technology Notes
PPP Handles auth + encryption via private key & certificate; non-routable by itself
PPTP Lets PPP data leave the network; easy to set up but weakly encrypted
IPSec Encrypts using the IP framework; harder to configure but strong & widely supported

Port Forwarding

Port forwarding (configured at the router) makes an internal service reachable from the Internet by opening a specific port and mapping the public IP to an internal host.

Port forwarding ≠ firewall

Port forwarding opens a port; a firewall decides whether traffic may travel through it, even when it's open.

4 · How the Web Works

DNS — Domain Name System

DNS translates human names (tryhackme.com) into IP addresses (104.26.10.229) so you don't memorise numbers.

The Domain Hierarchy

Domain name parts

  • TLD (Top-Level Domain): the rightmost part. gTLD (.com, .org) or ccTLD (.co.uk, .ca).
  • Second-Level Domain: e.g. tryhackme — max 63 chars, only a-z 0-9 -.
  • Subdomain: left of the SLD (admin.tryhackme.com), same rules, whole name ≤ 253 chars.

A DNS Request's Journey

DNS Record Types

Record Resolves to Example
A IPv4 address 104.26.10.229
AAAA IPv6 address 2606:4700:20::681a:be5
CNAME Another domain name store.* → shops.shopify.com
MX Mail servers (with priority) alt1.aspmx.l.google.com
TXT Free text (SPF, domain verification) anti-spam records

HTTP & HTTPS

HTTP vs HTTPS

HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the rulebook for requesting web resources. HTTPS is the same but encrypted — stopping eavesdropping and proving you're talking to the genuine server.

URL Anatomy

http://user:password@tryhackme.com:80/view-room?id=1#task3
└┬─┘   └──────┬─────┘ └─────┬──────┘└┬┘└───┬────┘└──┬──┘└─┬─┘
scheme     user:pass       host     port  path    query  fragment

Request / Response

GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: tryhackme.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 Firefox/87.0

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx/1.15.8
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 98

HTTP Methods

Method Intent
GET Retrieve information
POST Submit data / create records
PUT Update information
DELETE Remove records

Status Codes

Range Meaning Common codes
100–199 Informational 100 Continue
200–299 Success 200 OK · 201 Created
300–399 Redirection 301 Moved Permanently · 302 Found
400–499 Client errors 400 Bad Request · 401 Not Authorised · 403 Forbidden · 404 Not Found · 405 Method Not Allowed
500–599 Server errors 500 Internal Error · 503 Service Unavailable

Headers & Cookies

Request header Tells the server…
Host Which site (one server hosts many)
User-Agent Your browser & version
Content-Length How much data to expect
Cookie Your stored session data
Response header Tells the browser…
Set-Cookie Data to store & resend each request
Cache-Control How long to cache
Content-Type Data type (HTML, image, JSON…)

Cookies

HTTP is stateless — it forgets you between requests. A cookie (saved from a Set-Cookie header) is resent on every request so the server remembers who you are. Auth cookies hold a token (a secret code), not your password.

How Websites Are Built

Language Job
HTML Building blocks (tags/elements) define structure: <html><head><body><h1><p>
CSS Styling via class attributes
JavaScript Interactivity; dynamically updates the page (document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "…")

Front End vs Back End

  • Front End (client-side): what your browser renders (HTML/CSS/JS).
  • Back End (server-side): code you can't see (PHP, Python, Ruby, NodeJS…) that processes requests, talks to databases, and produces the HTML.

Two Classic Web Vulnerabilities

HTML Injection

When a site displays unfiltered user input, an attacker can inject their own HTML/JavaScript. The browser runs it — letting them control the page's look and behaviour. Rule: never trust user input — sanitise it.

Sensitive Data Exposure

Developers sometimes leave credentials, hidden links or secrets in the page source or JavaScript. Always View Page Source when assessing a site. (These labs lead directly into the Advent of Cyber web labs: XSS, IDOR and more.)

Other Web Components

Component Role
Web server (Apache, Nginx, IIS, NodeJS) Serves content from a root dir (/var/www/html, C:\inetpub\wwwroot); uses virtual hosts to serve many sites
Load Balancer Spreads traffic across servers (round-robin / weighted) + health checks for failover
CDN Hosts static files on thousands of global servers; serves the nearest copy
Database Stores data (MySQL, MSSQL, MongoDB, Postgres)
WAF (Web Application Firewall) Sits in front of the server; blocks attacks, bots & abuse via rate limiting

Static vs Dynamic content

Static content never changes (images, CSS). Dynamic content is generated per-request by back-end code (a blog homepage showing the latest post). Dynamic processing is where most web vulnerabilities live.

5 · Linux Fundamentals

Linux powers servers, security tools, Android, and most of the systems you'll attack or defend. Mastery of the terminal (text-based interface) is non-negotiable — it's faster, scriptable, and many tools are CLI-only.

Core Navigation & Files

Command Name Does
pwd print working directory Show where you are
ls list List directory contents (ls -a hidden, ls -l details, ls -al both)
cd change directory Move (cd .. up one level)
cat concatenate Output a file's contents
echo — Print text
whoami — Show current user
find — Search for files (find -name *.txt, * = wildcard)
grep — Search inside files for a pattern
touch — Create an empty file
mkdir make directory Create a folder
cp / mv / rm copy / move / remove Manage files (rm -R for folders)
file — Determine a file's real type 
grep "81.143.211.90" access.log   # find every log line for an IP
find -name "*.txt"                 # every .txt in/below current dir
wc -l access.log                   # count lines

Shell Operators

Operator Effect
& Run a command in the background
&& Run the next command only if the first succeeded
> Redirect output to a file (overwrite)
>> Redirect output to a file (append) 
echo hey > welcome     # creates/overwrites "welcome" with "hey"
echo hello >> welcome  # appends "hello" on a new line

Flags, Switches & the Manual

Most commands accept flags (-a), have a --help option, and a full man page: man ls. The manual is your first stop — see also Search Skills.

Permissions & Users

ls -l shows permission strings like -rw-r--r--: read, write, execute — split across owner / group / others.

Switching users

su user2 switches user; su -l user2 starts a login shell inheriting that user's environment and home directory. Privilege escalation often means moving toward root (the all-powerful user) via sudo su.

Filesystem Layout

Directory Holds
/etc System config — includes passwd, shadow (hashed passwords, SHA-512), sudoers
/var Variable data — logs live in /var/log
/root The root user's home
/tmp Temporary, volatile (cleared on reboot); world-writable — handy for staging attack scripts

Useful Utilities

Command Use
wget <url> Download a file over HTTP
scp src user@ip:/dest Securely copy files over SSH
python3 -m http.server Instantly serve current dir on port 8000
ssh user@ip Encrypted remote shell (see below)

SSH

Secure Shell encrypts a remote terminal session. Everything you type is encrypted in transit and decrypted on the remote host. The in-browser TryHackMe machines use this exact protocol. When typing an SSH password you see no stars or dots — that's normal.

Processes

Programs running on the machine. The kernel manages them; each has a PID.

Command Use
ps / ps aux List processes (aux = all users + system)
top Real-time process stats
kill <PID> Send a signal to end a process

Kill signals

SIGTERM — end, allowing cleanup · SIGKILL — end immediately, no cleanup · SIGSTOP — pause/suspend.

Process 0 boots the system (systemd on Ubuntu); everything else is a child of it. Manage services with systemctl start|stop|enable|disable apache2. Foreground/background: & or Ctrl+Z to background, fg to foreground.

Automation — Cron

cron runs scheduled tasks. A crontab line has 6 fields:

MIN  HOUR  DOM  MON  DOW  CMD
0    */12  *    *    *    cp -R /home/cmnatic/Documents /var/backups/

crontab -e to edit · * is a wildcard ("any"). (Online generators like crontab-generator.org help.)

Package Management

Software is installed from apt repositories. Add a trusted third-party repo with its GPG key, drop a .list file in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/, then apt update and apt install <pkg>. Remove with apt remove.

Logs & Text Editors

  • Logs live in /var/log (Apache access/error, fail2ban, UFW firewall) — vital for monitoring health and security.
  • Nano is the beginner-friendly editor (^ = Ctrl, ^X to exit). VIM is more powerful (syntax highlighting, customisable) but steeper.

6 · Windows Fundamentals

Windows dominates home and corporate networks, making it the biggest attack target. These notes cover its filesystem, admin tools, and built-in security.

The File System — NTFS

Modern Windows uses NTFS (New Technology File System), a journaling filesystem that can self-repair using a log. It replaced FAT16/FAT32 and HPFS (FAT still appears on USB sticks/SD cards).

NTFS feature Notes
Large files Supports files > 4 GB
Permissions Full control · Modify · Read & Execute · List folder contents · Read · Write (set via Properties → Security)
Compression & Encryption Folder/file compression; EFS encryption
Alternate Data Streams (ADS) Every file has a $DATA stream; extra hidden streams can store data — abused by malware to hide payloads; also used to tag Internet-downloaded files

Key Admin Tools

Tool (run command) Purpose
System Configuration (msconfig) Diagnose startup issues (General/Boot/Services/Startup/Tools). Needs admin; not a startup manager — use Task Manager for that.
Computer Management (compmgmt) Hub for Task Scheduler (run tasks automatically), Event Viewer (audit trail of events), Shared Folders (incl. default C$, ADMIN$), Services, Disk Management, Perfmon, Device Manager
System Information (msinfo32) Hardware resources, components, software environment, environment variables
Resource Monitor (resmon) Real-time per-process CPU/disk/network/memory

Services & Startup types

A service is a special application that runs in the background. Its Startup type (Automatic / Manual / Disabled) decides when it runs. Event Viewer logs five event types and standard logs under Windows Logs.

Environment variables

Store OS/program info — e.g. WINDIR holds the Windows install path. View via Advanced System Settings → Environment Variables.

Windows Security Features

Windows Update

Security fixes and patches arrive on Patch Tuesday (2nd Tuesday monthly); critical fixes can come sooner. control /name Microsoft.WindowsUpdate to open.

Windows Defender Firewall

Three profiles:

Profile Used for
Domain Networks where the host can authenticate to a domain controller
Private Home / trusted networks
Public Untrusted (coffee-shop Wi-Fi, airports) — the default

Open advanced rules with WF.msc. Leave the firewall on unless you're 100% sure.

Virus & Threat Protection (Defender AV)

  • Exclusions — skip files/folders in scans (reduces false positives, but excluded items could hide threats).
  • Ransomware protection — Controlled folder access (requires real-time protection on).
  • On-demand scan: right-click → Scan with Microsoft Defender.

Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS)

VSS creates consistent shadow copies (restore points) on protected drives. You can create restore points, perform system restore, configure or delete them.

Malware & shadow copies

Ransomware authors know about VSS and delete shadow copies so victims can't recover without paying. This is a classic indicator in ransomware incidents.

7 · Virtualization & Cloud

Virtualization

Before virtualization the rule was "one server = one application" — expensive, wasteful (5–20 % utilisation), slow to deploy, hard to scale. Virtualization lets multiple applications safely share one physical server.

The building analogy

  • Building = the physical server
  • Apartments = virtual machines (VMs)
  • Tenants = applications / operating systems
  • Building manager = the hypervisor that divides it safely
Concept What it is
Hypervisor Software that creates & manages VMs, allocating CPU/RAM/storage and keeping them isolated
Type 1 Runs directly on hardware — fast, for servers/data centres
Type 2 Runs inside an existing OS (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation) — easy, for learning/testing/malware labs
Virtual Machine A whole virtual computer with its own OS, fully isolated
Container Lightweight, isolated environment for one app that shares the host kernel — starts instantly, uses fewer resources, but must match the host OS type
Container image Pre-packed template used to create containers (Docker)

Malware testing safety

Use an isolated VM (often a different guest OS than your host) to test malicious files so the host isn't infected — Type 2 hypervisors are ideal. This ties into Malware Analysis and Containers.

VM vs Container in one line: a VM is the full apartment (max isolation, heavier); a container is a room inside it (lightweight, fast, scalable).

Cloud Computing

The cloud runs apps on provider infrastructure instead of your own hardware, built on virtualization & containers.

Benefits

Scalability · On-demand self-service · Pay only for what you use · Security · High availability · Global access.

Deployment types

Type Who uses it Why
Public Cloud Startups, global apps Affordable, easy to scale, no infra to manage
Private Cloud Banks, healthcare, government More control, compliance for sensitive data
Hybrid Cloud E-commerce Keep sensitive data private, scale publicly on demand

Service models — the "renting a home" analogy

Model You manage Example
IaaS OS + apps (rent raw compute) AWS EC2 virtual machines
PaaS Just your application App platforms
SaaS Nothing — just use it Gmail, Zoom

AWS terms from the lab

EC2 = a virtual computer in the cloud (has CPU/RAM, runs apps). Instance type (t2, t3, m5) sets its power/cost — bigger = more power + higher cost. Stopping unused instances immediately cuts billing. (This foundation leads into AWS Security.)

Major vendors: AWS (leader), Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud (GCP), Alibaba Cloud, IBM Cloud, Oracle Cloud. Netflix, Spotify and Instagram run on the cloud to scale globally and focus on product over hardware.

8 · Data Representation, Encoding & Programming

Number Systems

Computers understand two states (low/high voltage) → binary. We group bits for readability.

System Base Digits Groups
Decimal 10 0–9 everyday
Binary 2 0, 1 1 bit
Hexadecimal 16 0–F 4 bits per digit
Octal 8 0–7 3 bits per digit

Bit & Byte

A bit is one binary digit (0/1). A byte (a.k.a. octet) is 8 bits and represents 256 states.

Binary → decimal (positional, powers of 2):

1001 = 1×2³ + 0×2² + 0×2¹ + 1×2⁰ = 8 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 9
Dec Hex Binary
9 9 1001
10 A 1010
12 C 1100
15 F 1111

Representing Colour

Each pixel mixes Red, Green, Blue. With 1 bit each you get 2³ = 8 colours; with 8 bits (256 levels) each you get 256³ ≈ 16 million. A colour is therefore 3 bytes (24 bits), written as 6 hex digits — e.g. green A3EA2A instead of 10100011 11101010 00101010.

Character Encoding

Representation vs Encoding

Representation = data living as bits/numbers in memory. Encoding = the agreed mapping between numbers and meanings (which number is "A").

Encoding Covers Notes
ASCII (1963) English letters, digits, punctuation (0–127) 7-bit; A=65/0x41, a=97/0x61
ISO-8859-1 / -2 Western / Central-European letters Extended single-byte sets
Unicode Every writing system (~157 k chars) Code points like U+0041 (A), U+03A9 (Ω), U+1F525 (🔥)
UTF-8 Unicode in 1–4 bytes Most common on the web
UTF-16 / UTF-32 2–4 / fixed 4 bytes Common in Windows / simplest-but-wasteful

Why gibberish happens

If a file saved as one encoding is read as another, non-English characters display wrong — the classic cause of mojibake. Sender and receiver must agree on the encoding. This underpins decoding work in CyberChef and Obfuscation.

"TryHackMe" in ASCII binary: 01010100 01110010 01111001 01001000 01100001 01100011 01101011 01001101 01100101.

Databases & SQL

A database stores information in tables (like spreadsheets): columns are fields (types of info), rows are records.

Keyword Does
SELECT * Choose all columns (* = all)
FROM Orders Pick the table
WHERE drink = 'Coffee' Filter matching rows
ORDER BY price DESC Sort (DESC = high→low) 
SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE drink = 'Coffee' ORDER BY price DESC;

SQL & security

A query reads data; it doesn't change it. But if user input is dropped unsanitised into a query, an attacker can manipulate it — SQL injection (seen in the AI-in-Security and web labs). Always use parameterised queries.

Programming Essentials (JS & Python)

Both notes build the same "guess the number" game, illustrating three universals:

Concept JavaScript Python
Variable (changeable) let guess = 0; guess = 0
Constant (fixed) const secret = …; — (secret = …)
Conditional if / else if / else if / elif / else
Loop while (guess !== secret) {…} while guess != secret:
Random Math.floor(Math.random()*20)+1 random.randint(1, 20)
Input await rl.question(...) input(...)
Output console.log(...) print(...) 
if guess < 1 or guess > 20:
    print("Out of range.")
elif guess < secret:
    print("Too low, try again.")
elif guess > secret:
    print("Too high, try again.")
else:
    print("You got it!")

Why this matters for security

Reading and lightly modifying scripts is a core skill — you'll analyse attacker PowerShell/VBScript, write YARA conditions, and automate attacks with Bash loops. You don't need to write apps from scratch, but you must be able to look at code and explain what it does.

9 · Command-Line Mastery

GUIs are intuitive; CLIs are faster, lighter, scriptable, and remote-friendly (SSH). This chapter covers the three shells you'll live in.

Linux Shells

What is a shell?

A shell interprets your typed commands. Most Linux distros default to Bash. The restaurant analogy: ordering from a menu (GUI) vs cooking it yourself (CLI) — the CLI gives full control.

Shell Full name Standout features
Bash Bourne Again Shell Default everywhere; tab completion, history, strong scripting
Fish Friendly Interactive Shell Auto-suggestions, spell-correct, syntax highlighting built-in; beginner-friendly
Zsh Z Shell Advanced completion, oh-my-zsh themes/plugins, highly customisable

echo $SHELL shows your shell · cat /etc/shells lists installed shells · chsh -s /usr/bin/zsh changes default.

Shell Scripting

A script is a reusable set of commands in a .sh file.

#!/bin/bash                 # shebang: which interpreter to use
echo "Hey, what's your name?"
read name                   # take input
echo "Welcome, $name"       # $name = variable

Make it executable and run: chmod +x script.sh then ./script.sh (the ./ tells the shell to run this file).

Windows Command Prompt (cmd.exe)

Task Command
OS version ver
Full system info systeminfo
Env / path set
Help / clear help, cls, command /?
List dir dir (/a hidden, /s subdirs), tree
Create / remove dir mkdir, rmdir
View / copy / move / delete file type, copy, move, del/erase

Networking: ipconfig (/all for DNS/DHCP) · ping · tracert (trace route) · nslookup · netstat (-abon: all, binaries, owner PID, numeric). Processes: tasklist (filter with /FI "imagename eq sshd.exe") · taskkill /PID <pid>. Pipe long output through more (driverquery | more).

Windows PowerShell

The power in PowerShell

Unlike text-based cmd, PowerShell passes objects (data + properties + methods) between commands. Cmdlets follow a Verb-Noun convention (Get-Content, Set-Location), built on .NET; cross-platform since PowerShell Core (2016).

Cmdlet Equivalent Does
Get-ChildItem dir/ls List files
Set-Location cd Change directory
New-Item / Remove-Item create / del+rmdir Create / delete
Copy-Item / Move-Item copy / move Copy / move
Get-Content type/cat Read a file
Get-Command / Get-Help / Get-Alias — Discover cmdlets, docs, shortcuts

Piping, filtering & sorting

Get-ChildItem | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 1
Get-ChildItem | Where-Object -Property "Extension" -eq ".txt"
Select-String -Path ".\file.txt" -Pattern "hat"   # grep / findstr

Comparison operators: -eq -ne -gt -ge -lt -le -like.

Real-time system analysis (blue-team gold)

Cmdlet Reveals
Get-ComputerInfo Full system snapshot
Get-LocalUser Local accounts
Get-Process / Get-Service Running processes / services
Get-NetTCPConnection Active TCP connections (C2 hunting)
Get-NetIPConfiguration / Get-NetIPAddress Network config
Get-FileHash File hash (integrity / malware ID)
Get-Item -Path x -Stream * View Alternate Data Streams

Why analysts love PowerShell

Invoke-Command -ScriptBlock { … } runs commands on remote hosts — powering automation for incident response, threat hunting, and system administration. Red teams also use it for enumeration and remote execution, which is exactly why defenders watch for obfuscated/encoded PowerShell (see Web Attack Forensics).

The modern ss command

On Linux, netstat is deprecated in favour of ss (socket statistics, in iproute2) — faster, talks directly to the kernel. Map: netstat -a→ss -a, -t→ss -t (TCP), -l→ss -l (listening), -ltnp→ss -ltnp. Routing table → ip route; interface stats → ip -s link.

10 · Search Skills & Vulnerability Research

Knowing how to find answers is itself a core skill. This chapter covers evaluating sources, search operators, specialised engines, and vulnerability databases.

Evaluating Search Results

Anyone can publish anything online, so weigh information by:

  • Source — reputable, authoritative author/org?
  • Evidence & reasoning — backed by hard facts and logic?
  • Objectivity & bias — impartial, multiple perspectives?
  • Corroboration — confirmed by multiple independent reliable sources?

Snake oil

A cryptographic method/product that's bogus or ineffective. Red flags: "unbreakable"/"100 % secure" claims, secret proprietary algorithms (instead of vetted public standards like AES), vague "military-grade" marketing, and weak implementation.

Search Engine Operators

Harness advanced searches (Google / Bing / DuckDuckGo):

Operator Effect Example
"exact phrase" Exact match "passive reconnaissance"
site: Limit to a domain site:tryhackme.com success
- Exclude a term pyramids -giza
filetype: Find a file type filetype:pdf cyber

Specialised Search Engines

Engine Finds
Shodan Specific device/server types & versions exposed online (ICS, IoT)
Censys Hosts, websites, and certificates
VirusTotal Multi-engine virus scan of files/URLs + community notes
Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) Whether an email appears in a data breach

Technical Documentation

Official docs are the most accurate source:

  • Linux man pages — man ip (press q to quit); also searchable online.
  • Microsoft Learn — official Windows/command docs (ipconfig, etc.).
  • Product docs — Snort, Apache, etc.

Vulnerabilities & Exploits

CVE

Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — a dictionary giving each flaw a standard identifier, maintained by MITRE. Look them up at cve.org or the NVD (nvd.nist.gov).

Exploit code — ethics first

The Exploit Database, GitHub PoCs, and similar hold working exploit code. Only run exploits against systems you are explicitly authorised to test. (This mindset carries into every offensive lab in Part IV.)

11 · Windows Domains & Active Directory

Managing five computers individually is fine; managing 157 computers and 320 users across four offices is not. A Windows domain centralises administration — and Active Directory is the heart of it.

Windows Domains & AD DS

Why domains exist

A Windows domain is a group of users and computers under one business's administration. Main advantages: centralised identity management (configure all users from one place) and managing security policies (apply settings network-wide). You've met this at school/uni — one login works on every campus machine.

Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is the catalogue holding every object on the network.

Object Notes
Users Security principals (can authenticate & hold privileges). Represent people or services (IIS, MSSQL).
Machines Created per joined computer; name ends in $ (e.g. DC01$); local admin on their own host; 120-char auto-rotating password.
Security Groups Assign rights to whole groups. Defaults: Domain Admins, Server Operators, Backup Operators, Account Operators, Domain Users, Domain Computers, Domain Controllers.
OUs Organise objects (often mirroring departments: IT, Sales…) to apply policy. Default containers: Builtin, Computers, Domain Controllers, Users, Managed Service Accounts.

OUs vs Security Groups

OUs apply policies to users/computers (one object lives in one OU). Security Groups grant permissions over resources (an object can be in many groups). Different jobs entirely.

Authentication: Kerberos & NetNTLM

All domain credentials live on the Domain Controllers. When you authenticate to a service, it asks the DC to verify you — via one of two protocols.

Kerberos (modern default)

Kerberos tickets

  • TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) — proof of initial auth; encrypted with the krbtgt account hash.
  • TGS (Ticket Granting Service) — grants access to one specific service; encrypted with the service owner hash.
  • KDC (Key Distribution Center) — the DC service that issues tickets.

NetNTLM (legacy challenge-response)

Kept for compatibility. The client proves it knows the password without sending it:

  1. Client requests access → 2. Server sends a random challenge → 3. Client returns challenge + NTLM hash response → 4. Server forwards to DC → 5. DC recomputes & compares → 6. Result returned.

Why this matters offensively

Kerberos and NetNTLM are the backbone of countless AD attacks (Pass-the-Hash, Kerberoasting). The hash is never transmitted directly — attacks target the tickets and hashes instead. Pass-the-Hash detection appears in the Pyramid of Pain.

Group Policy Objects (GPOs)

A GPO is a collection of settings linked to OUs (or the whole domain) to push configuration — for users or computers.

Worked examples from the lab:

Goal Policy Linked to
Block non-IT from Control Panel Prohibit Access to Control Panel and PC settings (User Config) Marketing, Management, Sales OUs
Auto-lock idle screens after 5 min Machine inactivity limit (Computer Config) Root domain (inherited by child OUs; user-only OUs ignore computer settings)

Manage via Group Policy Management; GPOs sync through the SYSVOL network share.

Trees, Forests & Trusts

As companies grow, one domain isn't enough.

Concept Meaning
Tree Multiple domains sharing one namespace (thm.local → uk.thm.local, us.thm.local)
Forest Multiple trees with different namespaces joined (after a merger: thm.local + mht.local)
Enterprise Admins Group with admin rights across all domains in an enterprise
Trust Relationship Lets a user in one domain access resources in another

Trust direction

A one-way trust: if AAA trusts BBB, a user on BBB can access resources on AAA — the trust direction is opposite to the access direction. Joining domains in a tree/forest creates two-way trusts by default. A trust allows authorisation; it doesn't automatically grant access.

12 · Attack Vectors: Humans & Systems

Every attack needs a way in. Broadly, adversaries target people or systems — usually to gain access, then steal data, deploy ransomware, or destroy information.

Humans as an Attack Vector

Why attack humans?

"Breach through the gate, or just ask the gatekeeper to open the door." Humans provide access — to mailboxes, websites, databases. All human-targeted attacks rely on social engineering: manipulating psychology, not technology. Two ingredients: appear trustworthy, and trigger an emotion (urgency, fear, curiosity).

Breached target Attacker's next step
HR manager's Google account Steal & sell the employee database
Wealthy individual runs malware Hijack their web-banking session
IT administrator's VPN account Reach the heart of the corporate network

Defending humans

Mitigation How it helps
Anti-phishing solution Blocks phishing before users see it
Antivirus / EDR Stops users running malware
"Trust but verify" Verify suspicious "CEO/IT" requests via another channel
Security awareness training Teach phishing detection + simulations

The SOC analyst's job

You can't stop every attempt — your job is to detect and investigate. Detection is the theme of the rest of Part III.

Systems as an Attack Vector

What is a system?

Where data lives and runs: a physical server, a VM, or a cloud platform (Microsoft 365). Breaching one can mean data theft, ransomware, or defacement.

Vulnerabilities

Every piece of software has flaws; 40,000+ CVEs were published in 2024. Once public, a CVE starts a race: attackers build exploits, defenders deploy patches.

Responding to a CVE

The answer is always a patch from the vendor. Before one exists (zero-day), buy time by: restricting access to trusted IPs, applying vendor workarounds, and blocking known attack patterns on IPS/WAF. Examples: Shellshock, EternalBlue (2017), PrintNightmare (2021), Follina.

Misconfigurations

Not a software bug — a setup mistake by the IT team (weak passwords like 1111, exposed databases, misconfigured AWS). Often spotted only after exploitation.

Proactive defence What it does
Penetration testing Ethical hackers simulate attacks & report flaws
Vulnerability scans Detect default passwords / outdated software
Configuration audits Match systems to best practices (CIS benchmarks)

Supply chain

Your apps depend on thousands of libraries. If attackers compromise one and push a malicious update, everyone who installs it is hit — hard to defend because you can't control all upstream software.

13 · The SOC & Blue Team Structure

What is the Blue Team?

The Blue Team is defensive security — constantly monitoring for attacks and responding fast. Its size and shape depend on the company, but the SOC is where most careers begin.

SOC

The Security Operations Center — an organisation's defensive hub, often 24/7/365. The first line of defence, it works through alerts and handles most attacks. A typical day: review alerts, investigate anomalies, respond to incidents.

SOC roles

Role Responsibility
L1 Analyst Triage alerts; escalate complex cases to L2 (you start here)
L2 Analyst Investigate advanced attacks
Engineer Configure & maintain security tools (EDR, SIEM)
Manager Run the SOC, report results upward

CIRT & specialised roles

When the SOC is overwhelmed, call CIRT (a.k.a. CSIRT/CERT) — the firefighters (e.g. JPCERT, Mandiant, AWS CIRT). Larger orgs add specialists: Digital Forensics Analyst, Threat Intelligence Analyst, AppSec Engineer, AI Researcher.

The Security Hierarchy

Priorities differ per company: a law firm protects document confidentiality; a factory, production availability; a hospital, patient safety. Top executives (CEO) focus on business; they hire a CISO (Chief Information Security Officer) to lead security.

Your SOC Career Path

Internal SOC vs MSSP

Internal SOC MSSP (Managed Security Service Provider)
Example Protect your own company (a bank) Protect 60 customers for a provider
Pace Calmer shifts Often starts with a queue of urgent alerts
Tools A few, known deeply Many diverse platforms
Incident practice Rarer, deeper Weekly — learn from constant attacks

Four habits of a good analyst

Learn from every alert · think like an attacker · verify everything · never stop learning. Your natural next step after L1 is L2, but engineering, IR, or threat intel may call to you instead.

14 · Core SOC Tools: SIEM · EDR · SOAR

Three tool classes define the modern SOC. SIEM centralises and correlates logs; EDR watches the endpoints; SOAR automates the whole workflow.

SIEM — Security Information & Event Management

The problem SIEM solves

Networks produce hundreds of events per second across scattered devices in different formats. Analysing them individually is impossible: no centralisation, limited context, limited analysis, format chaos.

Log source types

Type Generated by Examples
Host-centric Windows, Linux, servers File access, authentication, process execution, registry edits, PowerShell
Network-centric Firewalls, IDS/IPS, routers SSH, FTP, web traffic, VPN logins, file sharing

What SIEM does

Centralised collection · Normalisation (raw logs → consistent fields) · Correlation (links events across sources) · Real-time alerting · Dashboards & reporting.

Correlation example

Individually harmless events — Haris logs in via VPN from a new IP → accesses a shared drive → runs a PowerShell script → system makes an outbound connection — correlated, they point to data exfiltration from compromised VPN creds.

Detection rules & alert investigation

If LogSource = WinEventLog AND EventID = 104  → alert "Event Log Cleared"
If LogSource = WinEventLog AND EventCode = 4688 AND NewProcessName contains "whoami"
                                               → alert "WHOAMI Execution Detected"

After an alert fires, decide: False Positive (tune the rule) · True Positive (investigate) · contact the asset owner · isolate host · block IP.

Log ingestion methods

Agent/Forwarder (Splunk forwarder) · Syslog · Manual upload (offline data) · Port-forwarding (SIEM listens on a port).

EDR — Endpoint Detection & Response

AV vs EDR — the airport analogy

Antivirus = immigration check: stops known criminals (signatures) but waves through an innocent-looking newcomer. EDR = security officers inside the airport, watching behaviour continuously and acting on anything suspicious. EDR adds behavioural detection over AV's signatures.

AV vs EDR through one attack

Attack step AV response EDR response
Phishing Word doc downloaded Nothing (no signature) Logs & monitors the download
User opens document Nothing (winword.exe is legit) Records execution, keeps watching
Macro spawns PowerShell Nothing (no signature) Flags the unusual winword→PowerShell parent-child
Obfuscated PowerShell downloads payload Usually nothing Flags obfuscated script
Payload injected into svchost.exe Nothing (no memory monitoring) Detects process injection
Attacker gets remote access No network visibility Flags svchost.exe's outbound connection
Final May mark clean Generates an alert with the full attack chain

The three pillars & telemetry

Telemetry collected (the endpoint's "black box"): process executions/terminations · network connections · command-line activity · file/folder modifications · registry modifications.

Detection techniques: Behavioural · Anomaly (learns a baseline) · IOC matching · MITRE ATT&CK mapping · Machine Learning (catches fileless/multi-stage chains).

Response actions: Isolate Host · Terminate Process · Quarantine file · Remote Access (RTR shell) · Artefact collection (memory dump, event logs, registry hives).

EDR's limit

EDR is host-only — it does not see network-level threats. That's why it works alongside SIEM, NDR, and firewalls.

SOAR — Security Orchestration, Automation & Response

What SOAR fixes

Traditional SOCs suffer alert fatigue, too many disconnected tools, manual processes, and talent shortage. SOAR unifies all tools so analysts don't switch between SIEM, EDR, firewall, TI and ticketing.

A VPN brute-force playbook, automated

  1. SIEM sends the alert → 2. query SIEM for the user's historical logins → 3. verify the IP's reputation via Threat Intel → 4. if malicious, disable the user in IAM → 5. open a ticket with full details.

Playbook

A predefined workflow telling SOAR what to do for a category of alert. Playbooks are dynamic — each step's result chooses the next path (a phishing playbook, a CVE-patching playbook that fetches CVEs from advisory lists, creates a patch ticket, tests before production, and builds a mitigation plan if assets stay vulnerable).

Do SOC analysts still matter?

Yes. SOAR automates repetitive tasks but can't make judgement calls at critical decision points. Complex investigations still need a human.

Splunk & the Elastic Stack

Two SIEM platforms you'll actually touch.

Splunk

Three components:

Ingest data via Add Data → Upload (5 steps: select source → source type → input settings/index → review → done). Search with SPL (Search Processing Language). Home screen: Splunk Bar, Apps Panel (default Search & Reporting), Explore Splunk, Home Dashboard.

Elastic Stack (ELK)

Component Role
Elasticsearch Full-text search/analytics engine (stores JSON docs)
Logstash Ingest → filter/normalise → output
Beats Single-purpose host data-shippers
Kibana Web UI for analysis & dashboards

KQL — Kibana Query Language

Search in the Discover tab two ways: free-text (United* — * wildcard; KQL matches whole terms) and field-based (Source_ip : 238.163.231.224 AND UserName : Suleman). Logical operators AND / OR / NOT. Build Visualizations (tables, pie charts) and combine them into Dashboards. The Discover tab (logs, fields pane, index pattern, search bar, time filter, timeline) is where analysts spend most time.

15 · Cyber Defense Frameworks

Frameworks give defenders a shared language and a map of how attacks unfold. Master these four.

Cyber Kill Chain

Lockheed Martin's 2011 model (from a military concept) defines the 7 stages of an intrusion. Breaking any link disrupts the attack.

Key terms

Malware = software designed to damage/gain access · Exploit = code abusing a vulnerability · Payload = the malicious code that runs. Passive recon = no direct contact (WHOIS, social media); Active recon = direct (port scanning, social engineering). Email-harvesting tools: theHarvester, Hunter.io, OSINT Framework.

Unified Kill Chain (UKC)

Paul Pols' 2017 framework complements (not competes with) the Cyber Kill Chain, with 18 phases grouped into three goals — and crucially, it accepts attackers loop back and forth.

UKC benefit vs other frameworks
Modern (2017, updated 2022) MITRE's base is 2013
Very detailed (18 phases) Others have a handful
Covers the whole attack end-to-end Others cover limited phases
Models realistic back-and-forth Others assume linear flow

Threat modelling

Steps to improve a system's security: (1) identify systems/functions to secure, (2) assess vulnerabilities & how they'd be exploited, (3) plan to secure them, (4) add policies (e.g. an SDLC) to prevent recurrence. Frameworks: STRIDE, DREAD, CVSS. The UKC helps identify attack surfaces for modelling.

MITRE

MITRE is a non-profit maintaining several essential knowledge bases.

ATT&CK Framework

Tactic · Technique · Procedure

  • Tactic = the adversary's goal (the why) — e.g. Reconnaissance.
  • Technique = how they achieve it — e.g. Active Scanning.
  • Sub-technique = a specific method — e.g. Scanning IP Blocks.
  • Procedure = the actual implementation.

A globally-accessible knowledge base of adversary TTPs from real-world observations, covering Windows, macOS, Linux, cloud and more. The ATT&CK Matrix / Navigator visualise it.

Who uses ATT&CK How
CTI teams Map threat-actor behaviour to TTPs → actionable profiles
SOC Analysts Add context to alerts, prioritise incidents
Detection Engineers Map SIEM/EDR rules to ATT&CK for coverage
Incident Responders Map timelines to tactics/techniques
Red & Purple Teams Build emulation plans

MITRE's other projects

Project Purpose
CAR (Cyber Analytics Repository) Ready-made detection analytics with pseudocode + Splunk/LogPoint queries (e.g. CAR-2020-09-001)
D3FEND The defensive counterpart — maps defensive techniques (Model, Harden, Detect, Isolate, Deceive, Evict); e.g. Credential Rotation D3-CRO
Emulation Library / Caldera Adversary emulation plans & automated emulation tool
AADAPT / ATLAS Newer matrices for digital-asset payments / AI systems threats

The Pyramid of Pain

David Bianco's model ranks indicators by how much pain detecting them causes the attacker. The higher you detect, the harder (and more expensive) it is for them to adapt.

Indicator Pain Why
Hash values Trivial Change one bit → totally new hash (echo x >> file)
IP addresses Easy Attacker rotates IPs; Fast Flux evades blocking
Domain names Simple Must buy/register/change DNS; watch for Punycode & URL shorteners
Host artifacts Annoying Registry values, dropped files, suspicious process spawns
Network artifacts Annoying User-Agent strings, C2 URIs, HTTP POST patterns (detect in PCAPs with TShark)
Tools Challenging Detecting tools forces attacker to rebuild — use AV sigs, detection rules, YARA, fuzzy hashing (SSDeep)
TTPs Tough! Detecting behaviour (e.g. Pass-the-Hash) leaves them to retrain or give up

Bianco's principle

"The amount of pain you cause an adversary depends on the types of indicators you are able to make use of." Climbing the pyramid shifts you from blocking throwaway indicators to disrupting the attacker's very playbook. Hashing algorithms: MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2 (look up on VirusTotal / MetaDefender).

16 · Alert Triage, Reporting & Metrics

The day-to-day craft of an L1 analyst: turning a flood of alerts into decisions, documenting them, and measuring the team's effectiveness.

From Events to Alerts

Alert management platforms: SIEM (Splunk ES, Elastic) · EDR/NDR (MS Defender, CrowdStrike) · SOAR (Splunk/Cortex SOAR) · ITSM (Jira, TheHive).

Alert Properties

# Property Meaning
1 Alert Time When the alert was created (minutes after the event)
2 Alert Name Summary from the rule (e.g. Unusual Login Location)
3 Severity 🟢 Low · 🟡 Medium · 🟠 High · 🔴 Critical
4 Status 🆕 New · 🔄 In Progress · ✅ Closed
5 Verdict 🔴 True Positive · 🟢 False Positive
6 Assignee The owner responsible
7 Description Rule logic, why it's suspicious, how to triage
8 Fields Values that triggered it (hostname, command line…)

Alert Prioritisation & Triage

Prioritisation order

  1. Filter — only take new, unreviewed alerts. 2. Sort by severity — critical → high → medium → low. 3. Sort by time — oldest first (older breaches are further along).

Four triage factors (Advent of Cyber)

Factor Ask Why
Severity How bad? Urgency & business risk
Time When? Spot ongoing / repeated attacks
Context Where in the attack lifecycle? How far has the attacker progressed?
Impact Who/what is affected? Prioritise by asset importance

Investigation steps: investigate the alert in detail → check related logs → correlate multiple alerts (same user/IP/device reveals the attack path) → build a timeline → decide the next action → document findings.

Reporting & Escalation

Why L1 analysts write reports

  • Context for escalation — saves L2 huge time.
  • Records — raw SIEM logs last 3–12 months, but alerts are kept indefinitely.
  • Skill growth — "if you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it."

Report format — the Five Ws

W Capture
Who Which user logged in / ran the command / downloaded the file
What The exact action or event sequence
When Start & end of the suspicious activity
Where Device, IP, or website involved
Why (most important) your reasoning for the verdict

When to escalate to L2

  1. Indicator of a major cyberattack needing deeper investigation/DFIR.
  2. Remediation needed (malware removal, host isolation, password reset).
  3. Communication with customers/management/law enforcement required.
  4. You simply don't fully understand it — asking is better than blindly closing.

Steps: write report + verdict → move alert to In Progress → reassign to L2 on shift → ping them.

Communication edge cases

L2 unresponsive 30 min on a critical alert → call L2, then L3, then manager. Slack/Teams account compromise → verify the user via another channel (phone), never the breached chat. Realise you misclassified days later → tell L2 immediately (actors stay silent for weeks).

SOC Metrics & Objectives

Metric Formula Measures Common SLA
Alerts Count total alerts received Analyst workload —
False Positive Rate FP / total alerts Noise level —
Alert Escalation Rate escalated / total L1 experience —
Threat Detection Rate detected / total threats SOC reliability —
MTTD — Attack → detection 5 min
MTTA — Alert → triage starts 10 min
MTTR — Alert → breach stopped 60 min

Worked example

Alert after 12 min, moved to In Progress 10 min later, escalated after 6 min, L2 spent 35 min cleaning → MTTD 12, MTTA 10, MTTR 51 (12+6+... = 10 to ack; 12+6+35−... the room's answer: 12, 10, 51). A 94 % false-positive rate means analysts grow numb and miss real threats — tune rules.

SOC Workbooks & Lookups

Workbook / Playbook / Runbook

A structured document defining the steps to investigate & remediate a specific threat consistently — vital because L1 analysts are junior. Example: an Unusual Login Location workbook (enrichment → investigation → escalation).

To triage "G.Baker logged into HQ-FINFS-02 and shared a file with R.Lund," you need context from:

Lookup Holds Sources
Identity Inventory Users/services: role, contacts, privileges AD/Entra ID, SSO (Okta), HR systems, CSV/Excel
Asset Inventory Hosts: location, IP, OS, owner, purpose AD, SIEM/EDR, MDM (Intune/Jamf), CSV/Excel
Network Diagrams Subnets, firewall rules, services Documentation

A network diagram turns raw IPs into a story: an external IP brute-forces VPN (port 10443) → gets a VPN-subnet IP → scans the Database subnet (blocked by firewall) → pivots to the Office subnet.

17 · Offensive Web & AI Labs

Hands-on web-application attacks from Advent of Cyber 2025. Each builds on How the Web Works.

AI in Cyber Security

AI agents now assist across the whole field:

Area AI's role
Red (offensive) Automate recon/OSINT, analyse noisy scanner output, generate exploit scripts
Blue (defensive) Process telemetry continuously; speed detection, investigation & automated response (isolate device, block email)
Software A "virtual colleague"; SAST/DAST vuln-finding — ironically better at finding bugs than writing secure code

Considerations

You don't own AI output; decisions may be opaque or biased; it can be wrong. Never assume 100 % accuracy — especially in offensive testing where a mistake hits a real client.

The lab generated a SQL-injection exploit (username = "alice' OR 1=1 -- -"), analysed the resulting web log, and reviewed vulnerable PHP. Fix SQLi with prepared/parameterised queries and input sanitisation.

SQL Injection & Secure Coding

SQL Injection (SQLi)

When unsanitised user input is concatenated into a database query, an attacker can change the query's logic — bypassing login, reading other tables, or dumping the database. See Databases & SQL for the query basics.

Payload fragment Effect
' OR 1=1 -- - Makes the WHERE always true; -- comments out the rest
' UNION SELECT ... Appends attacker-chosen columns to the result
'; DROP TABLE ... Stacks a second, destructive statement

Why the vulnerable PHP failed

$user = $_POST['username'] ?? '' takes raw input and drops it straight into the query — no validation, no escaping. Any quote the attacker types becomes part of the SQL.

Secure-coding fixes (defence in depth):

Control What it does
Prepared / parameterised queries Data is bound separately from SQL — input can never become code (the single most important fix)
Input validation Reject anything not matching the expected format
Sanitisation / escaping filter_input, htmlspecialchars for defence in depth
Least-privilege DB account The web user can't DROP tables even if injected
WAF Blocks common injection patterns at the edge

Test it yourself

Tools like OWASP ZAP (scanning) and SQLmap (automated injection testing) confirm whether an endpoint is vulnerable — only against systems you're authorised to test.

IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference

IDOR (a.k.a. Authorization Bypass)

An access-control flaw: the app uses a reference (like /user/1) to fetch data but never checks you're allowed that object. Change the ID → see someone else's data.

Authentication vs Authorization

Authentication = verifying who you are (username + password → a cookie/token). Authorization = verifying what you're allowed. Authorization can't happen before authentication. IDOR is usually horizontal privilege escalation (same privilege level, other users' data) vs vertical (gaining more features).

IDOR disguises (still exploitable): plain numbers → encoding (Mg== = Base64 of 2) → hashes (MD5/SHA1 of a known value) → UUIDv1 (recoverable if you know the generation timestamp).

The fix

Check ownership server-side on every request — don't rely on hiding/encoding IDs. Use hard-to-guess IDs for public links as well, and log/monitor failed access attempts.

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

Injecting malicious JavaScript into input fields that get reflected to other users.

Type Where the script lives Victim
Reflected In the request/URL, echoed immediately Whoever clicks the crafted link (via phishing)
Stored Saved on the server (e.g. a comment) Every user who views the page — "set and forget" 
<!-- test payload -->
<script>alert('Meow Meow')</script>

Impact

Steal session cookies, trigger fake login popups, deface pages, or act as the victim.

Defences: use textContent not innerHTML · set cookies HttpOnly + Secure · sanitise & encode input/output · if HTML must be allowed, filter strictly.

Race Conditions

Race condition

When two+ actions happen simultaneously and the outcome depends on finishing order. In web apps, concurrent requests can manipulate stock or balances.

Type What happens
TOCTOU (Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use) Data changes between the check and the use
Shared resource Multiple writes to the same data without control
Atomicity violation A "do it all at once" operation runs in separable parts

The exploit (Burp Suite): make one legitimate checkout → capture the POST /process_checkout → send to Repeater → duplicate the tab ~15× into a group → Send group in parallel (last-byte sync) → stock goes negative, multiple orders confirm.

Mitigation

Atomic DB transactions · final stock validation before commit · idempotency keys · rate limiting / concurrency controls.

Exploitation with cURL

curl speaks HTTP from the command line — ideal when GUI tools aren't available.

curl http://MACHINE_IP/                               # GET
curl -X POST -d "username=user&password=user" .../post.php   # POST
curl -i -X POST -d "user=admin&pass=admin" .../post.php      # -i shows headers
curl -c cookies.txt -d "username=admin&password=admin" .../session.php  # save cookies
curl -b cookies.txt .../session.php                   # reuse cookies
curl -A "internalcomputer" .../ua_check.php           # spoof User-Agent

Brute-force loop (the logic behind Hydra / Burp Intruder / WFuzz):

for pass in $(cat passwords.txt); do
  response=$(curl -s -X POST -d "username=admin&password=$pass" http://MACHINE_IP/bruteforce.php)
  echo "$response" | grep -q "Welcome" && { echo "[+] Found: $pass"; break; }
done

Agentic AI & Prompt Injection

Agentic AI

AI with agency — it can plan multi-step tasks, act (run tools, call APIs, copy files), and watch & adapt. Powered by LLMs using Chain-of-Thought reasoning and the ReAct (Reason + Act) pattern — alternating reasoning traces with actions.

The risk

Tools are registered to the model via JSON schemas (e.g. web_search(query)). When an agent follows a process to complete tasks, attackers can interfere with that process through crafted input — prompt injection (plus jailbreaking and data poisoning) — forcing unsafe or unintended actions. Strong input handling and tool-permission controls are essential.

18 · Malware, Forensics & Detection Labs

The defensive hands-on core: analysing malware, decoding obfuscation, hunting in logs and the registry, and detecting C2.

Malware Analysis Fundamentals

The golden rule

Never run dangerous applications on devices you care about. Analyse samples inside a safe, isolated sandbox (usually a VM with snapshotting). See Virtualization.

Static analysis — what PeStudio reveals

Information Why it matters
Checksums Google the hash to see if it's known malware
Strings Readable text: IPs, URLs, commands, even passwords
Imports Libraries/functions it uses (e.g. CreateFileW) → how it interacts with the OS
Resources Icons & embedded data — malware hides here (fake Word icon)

Dynamic analysis tools

  • Regshot — snapshots the registry before/after to spot changes (malware adds a Run key for persistence).
  • ProcMon — monitors real-time process/registry/file/network interactions.

Obfuscation & CyberChef

Encoding vs Encryption vs Obfuscation

Encoding transforms data for compatibility (reversible, no key). Encryption protects confidentiality (needs a key). Obfuscation makes data hard to read to evade detection & delay analysis.

Technique Visual clue
ROT1 / ROT13 Words look "one/13 letters off"; spaces unchanged (the→gur)
Base64 Long alphanumeric strings, + /, ending =/==
XOR Random symbols, same length as original; short reused keys repeat

CyberChef — the Cyber Swiss Army Knife

Four areas: Operations (capabilities) → drag into Recipe (chain them) → Input → Output. Apply layered obfuscation in reverse order to recover plaintext. The Magic operation auto-guesses common decoders (won't catch custom XOR keys).

XOR's magic property

XOR-ing the result with the same key again returns the original data. Two XOR operations with one key = identity. Used to reverse XOR-encoded payloads (and in the CyberChef "lock" challenges, chained with Base64 and hashing → CrackStation for MD5).

HTA Malware Analysis

HTA files

HTML Application files run via mshta.exe — HTML + CSS + VBScript/JavaScript as a desktop app. Legitimately used for admin tools; abused for initial access, downloaders/droppers, obfuscation, and living-off-the-land (calling mshta.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe, rundll32.exe).

Three-step analysis process:

Check <title> & HTA:APPLICATION first (fake names like "Salary Survey"). Watch CreateObject() calls: InternetExplorer.Application (external connection), WScript.Network (recon), WScript.Shell (run commands). Trace variable chains — in the sample, $U (decoded URL) → $C (downloaded content) → $B (runs it as a scriptblock in memory).

Web Attack Forensics (Splunk)

Reconstruct an attack chain across log sources with SPL.

Query goal SPL
Suspicious web commands index=windows_apache_access (cmd.exe OR powershell OR "Invoke-Expression")
Server-side errors/exec index=windows_apache_error ("cmd.exe" OR "powershell" OR "Internal Server Error")
Apache spawning processes index=windows_sysmon ParentImage="*httpd.exe"
Enumeration confirmed index=windows_sysmon *cmd.exe* *whoami*
Encoded PowerShell index=windows_sysmon Image="*powershell.exe" (CommandLine="*enc*" OR "*-EncodedCommand*")

The smoking gun

If httpd.exe (Apache) spawns cmd.exe or powershell.exe, that's a command injection that reached the OS — Apache should only spawn worker threads. Decode Base64 PowerShell to see the attacker's true intent.

Windows Registry Forensics

The Windows Registry

The OS's "brain" — a database of all configuration, stored across several hives (files).

Hive Contains In Registry Editor
SYSTEM Services, drivers, boot, mounted devices HKLM\SYSTEM
SECURITY Local security & audit policy HKLM\SECURITY
SOFTWARE Installed programs, OS info, autostarts HKLM\SOFTWARE
SAM Usernames, password hashes, groups HKLM\SAM
NTUSER.DAT Recent files, user prefs, user autostarts HKU\<SID> / HKCU
USRCLASS.DAT Shellbags, jump lists HKU\<SID>\Software\Classes

Forensically useful keys: USBSTOR (connected USBs) · RunMRU (Run-dialog commands) · UserAssist (GUI-launched apps) · TypedPaths / WordWheelQuery (Explorer address bar / search) · Run (startup/persistence) · RecentDocs (recent files). Use Registry Explorer (Eric Zimmerman) for deep analysis — the built-in editor only shows live data.

C2 Detection with RITA

RITA + Zeek

RITA (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics) detects C2 communication by analysing network logs. It only accepts Zeek logs (Zeek is a network-security-monitoring tool, not an IDS). Convert a PCAP first: zeek readpcap capture.pcap output_dir/.

zeek readpcap pcaps/AsyncRAT.pcap zeek_logs/asyncrat   # PCAP → Zeek logs
rita import --logs ~/zeek_logs/asyncrat/ --database asyncrat
rita view asyncrat                                      # search bar: /  help: ?

RITA detects: C2 beaconing · DNS tunnelling · long connections · data exfiltration · threat-intel matches, scoring connections by severity.

Threat modifier Flags
MIME/URI mismatch Header MIME type ≠ URI
Rare signature Unusual user-agent/SSL cert
Prevalence Few internal hosts talk to one external host
First Seen New external host = more suspicious
Missing host header Attacker oversight
Large outgoing data Possible exfiltration

Reading results

Long FQDNs (sunshine-bizrate-inc-software[.]trycloudflare[.]com), non-standard ports, long durations, and high connection counts all point to C2. Pivot into the Zeek logs/PCAP and confirm malicious IPs on VirusTotal.

YARA Rules

YARA

A tool to identify & classify malware by matching patterns — a detective's notebook for defenders. Used for post-incident analysis, threat hunting, intel-based scans, and memory analysis.

Every rule has three parts:

rule TBFC_KingMalhare_Trace {
    meta:                                   // author, description, date
        author = "Defender of SOC-mas"
    strings:                                // the clues to search for
        $s1 = "rundll32.exe" fullword ascii
        $mz = { 4D 5A 90 00 }               // hex: MZ (Windows exe header)
    condition:                              // when to trigger
        $s1 and $mz
}
Element Role
Meta Info about the rule (optional but recommended)
Strings Text, hex, or regex clues
Conditions Logic that fires the rule

String modifiers: nocase (ignore case) · wide ascii (2-byte + 1-byte) · xor (all single-byte XOR variants) · base64. Conditions: $xmas · any of them · all of them · ($s1 or $s2) and not $benign · any of them and (filesize < 700KB).

yara -r icedid_starter.yar C:\    # -r recursive   -s show matched strings

19 · Infrastructure, Cloud & Tooling Labs

Network discovery, password attacks, containers, cloud, industrial systems, and phishing — the remaining Advent of Cyber hands-on labs.

Network Discovery with Nmap

The attack flow

  1. Know your target (IP). 2. Scan for open ports (22 SSH, 80 HTTP). 3. Explore the services behind them. 4. Exploit a way in.
nmap MACHINE_IP                 # top 1000 ports
nmap -p- MACHINE_IP             # all 65535 TCP ports
nmap -sU MACHINE_IP             # UDP ports (e.g. 53 DNS)
nmap -sV -p 22,80,502 IP        # service/version detection on specific ports
ss -tunlp                       # on-host: list listening ports (TCP/UDP/numeric/process)
Protocol Default port Note
SSH 22 Remote shell
HTTP 80 Web
FTP 21 (or custom, e.g. 21212) Try anonymous login
DNS 53/udp Hides data in records (dig @IP TXT name +short)
MySQL 3306 May allow unauthenticated localhost access

On-host discovery

Once you have a shell, don't scan — just ask the OS its listening ports with ss -tunlp (or netstat). With root you also see the owning process.

Password Attacks

Encryption's strength depends almost entirely on the password. Attackers don't break the crypto — they guess the password offline.

Attack How
Dictionary Try a wordlist (rockyou.txt, common-passwords.txt)
Mask Limit to a known format: ?l?l?l?d?d = 3 lowercase + 2 digits
Brute-force All combinations (slow; GPU-accelerated with hashcat) 
file flag.pdf                       # confirm file type first
pdfcrack -f flag.pdf -w rockyou.txt # crack a PDF
zip2john flag.zip > ziphash.txt     # extract a crackable hash
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt ziphash.txt

Detecting cracking on an endpoint

Offline cracking doesn't hit login services, so watch the host: process names (john, hashcat, fcrackzip, pdfcrack, zip2john) · command flags (--wordlist, -a 3, -m) · potfiles (~/.john/john.pot) · GPU spikes (nvidia-smi, nvcuda.dll/libcuda.so) · downloads of rockyou.txt/SecLists. Detect with Sysmon + Sigma rules.

Response playbook: isolate host → capture triage artefacts → preserve working dir/wordlists/history → review decrypted files → identify origin/intent → remediate & rotate keys/passwords, enforce MFA → educate.

Containers & Docker

See Virtualization for the fundamentals. Docker builds/runs/manages containers sharing the host kernel.

Container escape

A container escape lets code inside a container reach the host or other containers. If the Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) is mounted into a container, you can run Docker commands from inside it (docker ps) and reach a privileged container — then execute on the host. Mitigation: Enhanced Container Isolation blocks socket mounting.

docker ps                                # list running containers
docker exec -it uptime-checker sh        # shell into a container
ls -la /var/run/docker.sock              # check socket access
docker exec -it deployer bash            # pivot to a privileged container

AWS Security

IAM — Identity & Access Management

AWS's service for managing identities and their permissions.

IAM concept Meaning
User A single identity with credentials (password / access keys)
Group Many users bundled for easier access management
Role A temporary identity a user/service can assume for certain permissions
Policy JSON defining Action (allowed) · Resource · Condition · Principal (for whom)

Attacker enumeration flow (credentials in ~/.aws/credentials):

aws sts get-caller-identity                              # who am I?
aws iam list-users
aws iam list-user-policies --user-name sir.carrotbane    # inline policies
aws iam get-user-policy --policy-name X --user-name ...   # → found sts:AssumeRole
aws iam list-roles                                       # → found "bucketmaster"
aws iam get-role-policy --role-name bucketmaster --policy-name BucketMasterPolicy
aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:...:role/bucketmaster --role-session-name TBFC
# export the temp AccessKeyId / SecretAccessKey / SessionToken, then:
aws s3api list-buckets
aws s3api get-object --bucket easter-secrets-123145 --key cloud_password.txt out.txt

Inline vs Attached policies · S3

Inline policies are hard-coded into one identity (deleted with it); attached policies are reusable. S3 = Simple Storage Service, object storage for any file type.

Industrial Control Systems & Modbus

SCADA & PLC

SCADA (Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition) is the command centre of industrial operations — sensors/actuators, PLCs (Programmable Logic Controllers — rugged industrial computers running control logic), monitoring systems, and historians (data stores).

Modbus (1979) is the industrial request/response protocol — no authentication, no encryption, no authorisation. Modbus TCP listens on port 502.

Modbus data type I/O Values
Coils Digital output (writable) 0/1
Discrete Inputs Digital input (read-only) 0/1
Holding Registers Analogue output (writable) 0–65535
Input Registers Analogue input (read-only) 0–65535

The attack & safe remediation

King Malhare connected to port 502 (no auth) and rewrote registers/coils: HR0=1 (force eggs), HR4=666 (signature), C11=True (protection trap). Order matters — disable protection (C11) first, then change HR0, else C15 (self-destruct) arms a 30-second countdown that dumps inventory to Zone 10. Addresses are zero-indexed. Investigate with Python + pymodbus (read_holding_registers, read_coils). Real ICS malware: FrostyGoop (2024).

Phishing

The oldest trick, still the most effective — targeting people, the one thing technology can't patch. (See Humans as an Attack Vector.)

Spam vs Phishing

Spam = bulk digital noise (quantity over precision; promotion, scams, clickbait). Phishing = a precision strike to deceive specific users (credential theft, malware delivery, data exfiltration, financial fraud).

Techniques — at least one is always present:

SPF · DKIM · DMARC

Email-authentication checks in the Authentication-Results header. SPF lists servers allowed to send for a domain. DKIM adds a signature proving the message wasn't altered. DMARC uses both to decide what to do with fakes (spam/block). SPF + DMARC both fail = strong spoofing sign. Check Return-Path to spot the real sender and Punycode (ACE prefix).

Trending phishing moved from dropping malware to stealing access: abusing legitimate tools (Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive) to host lures → fake login pages → side-channel communication (SMS, WhatsApp, calls) to continue the con off-email.

21 · Your Learning Roadmap

Captured from your root "Where To Start" notes — practitioner advice on where to go after these foundations.

The core philosophy

"Honestly, spam as many CTF boxes as you can. It's less about memorising and more about knowing something exists." — e.g. "oh, 6379, I remember seeing that on a CTF" → check your notes → it's Redis → look at Redis exploits. And take good notes — they really help. (The author still uses their OSCP notes.)

The cheaper path

  1. Hack The Box — spam the oldest retired machines to newest. After ~50–75 you'll have a good grasp.
  2. CRTP (Certified Red Team Professional, Altered Security) — gives a strong Active Directory background and reflects real day-job work. Their ADCS course is great too.
  3. Then target OSCP or one of the Hack The Box certs.

Going deeper: C2 & modern defence evasion

For C2 frameworks or bypassing modern defences (AV/EDR):

  • Maldev Academy + Matt Hand's book (Evading EDR).
  • LitterBox — self-learning tool: github.com/BlackSnufkin/LitterBox.

Glossary from your notes

  • Red Team — offensive security.
  • Blue Team — cyber security & technology professionals protecting an information system from threats via defensive actions.
  • SOC — a team monitoring, preventing, detecting, investigating & responding to threats across a company's network/systems.
  • XOR — a binary operation for encryption/decryption; result is 1 if the two bits differ, 0 if the same.
  • Container — a package bundling code + dependencies so it runs reliably in any environment.
